newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX heat sends oil complex to sharply higher end.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX heat sends oil complex to sharply higher end.

text.p: All three legs of the NYMEX oil complex were sent to life-of-contract highs in the spot month by a heating oil rally Monday, and then held on to much of their gains to settle sharply higher.
The heating oil rally was touched off by forecasts for a cold spell in the U.S. Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world.
February heating oil ended 2.35 cents a gallon higher at 73.64 cents after setting a life-of-contract high of 74.50.
February gasoline finished up 1.82 cents at 72.52 cents a gallon after making a contract high of 72.90 cents.
February crude rose 88 cents a barrel intraday to a contract high of $26.47 before ending at $26.37, up 78 cents.
"Crude was carried up as the heating oil rally created more interest in crude," said Michael Busby, trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York.
The Northeast will experience much below normal temperatures by late week and into next week, weather forecasters said Monday.
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis in Chicago said temperatures could decline by 10 to 20 degrees below normal in the eastern one third of the nation from Friday to Monday.
Freese-Notis Weather, a private forecaster in Des Moines, Iowa, expected temperatures in parts of the Northeast to drop eight to 10 degrees below normal between January 12 and 16.
Crude was helped in part by news of tightening supply, dealers said.

With the post-Gulf War high of $26.80 made December 19 near at hand, Texaco said the amount of crude it was to buy from Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) has been reduced at SOMO's request.
"The contract has been reduced from 20,000 barrels a day to 10,000 barrels a day," a Texaco official said.

SOMO has reduced the amount of crude it will export in a number of contracts on concern that high oil prices might mean it would overshoot its sales limit of $1 billion of oil over three months under the "oil-for-food" deal with the United Nations.
In December, the United Nations approved a deal that eased sanctions against Iraq and allowed Iraq to export oil, under certain conditions, in exchange for food and other humanitarian aid.
"It's a psychological thing more than anything else. The amount of crude really is not that significant," Northville's Busby said of the Iraqi oil news.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk ((212-859-1761))
